title: Prospective association between screen use modalities and substance use experimentation in early adolescents
authors: Nagata JM, Shim J, Low P, Ganson KT, Testa A, He J, Santos GM, Brindis CD, Baker FC, Shao IY

primary_models.name: Weighted multiple logistic regression of Year 3 substance use experimentation on Year 2 phone/SM modality hours per day, adjusted for Year 2 substance experimentation and sociodemographic covariates
primary_models.location_in_paper: Fig. 1 (p. 4), forest plot with OR (95% CI) printed for each modality x outcome; described in Results p. 3; interpreted in Abstract and Discussion pp. 3-5.
primary_models.design: Prospective longitudinal analysis over two ABCD follow-up waves. Screen time modalities measured at the Year 2 follow-up (2018-2020, participants mostly 11-12 years old); substance use experimentation measured at the Year 3 follow-up, one year later. The same experimentation outcome at Year 2 is entered as a covariate. Single follow-up outcome per person (no repeated measures). Each outcome (alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, any substance) is a separate binary DV. The paper says 'multiple logistic regression models' were run and the forest plot lists one OR per modality; it does not state explicitly whether each modality was entered in its own model or all modalities together, but the format (total screen time and each component listed in parallel) is consistent with one modality per model.
primary_models.sample: ABCD Study, Year 2 and Year 3 follow-up data (release version not stated in the PDF). Analytic N = 8006 with complete screen time, substance use experimentation, and covariate data; included vs. excluded comparison is in online Appendix A (not bundled in this PDF), and the Discussion notes excluded participants were more likely to be from lower household income, lower parent education, and Latino, Black, Asian, or Other race/ethnicity. Weighted descriptives (Table 1, p. 3): mean age at Year 2 12.1 (SD 0.7); 47.9% female, 52.1% male; 58.4% White, 18.3% Latino/Hispanic, 13.7% Black, 5.1% Asian, 3.2% Native American, 1.3% Other; household income <$25K 14.7%, $25-49,999 20.1%, $50-74,999 18.3%, $75-99,999 14.3%, $100-199,999 24.6%, >=$200K 8.1%; parent education high school or less 14.8%, college or higher 85.2%.
primary_models.iv: Year 2 hours per day on one screen modality, from the ABCD Youth Screen Time Survey. Youth reported average daily time on weekdays and weekends for each of eight modalities; the qualifying ones here are texting, video chatting (e.g., Skype, Facetime), and social media (e.g., Facebook, Instagram, Twitter). Daily hours = ((weekday average x 5) + (weekend average x 2)) / 7. Entered continuously; OR is per additional hour per day. Weighted Year 2 means (SD), Table 1: texting 0.7 (1.5), social media 0.7 (1.6), video chat 0.5 (1.3) hours/day.
primary_models.dv: Year 3 youth-reported substance use experimentation, four binary outcomes analysed separately: alcohol (ever had a sip of alcohol such as beer, wine or liquor), nicotine (a puff from a tobacco or electronic cigarette, Juul, vape pen, e-hookah, cigar or pipe), cannabis (a puff or eaten any marijuana), and any substance use experimentation (tried any of the three). The alcohol sipping item is adapted from the iSay Sip Inventory. Weighted prevalence (Table 2, p. 3), Year 2 / Year 3: alcohol 10.4% / 12.0%; nicotine 1.0% / 2.5%; cannabis 0.3% / 1.0%; any substance 11.1% / 13.2%. Cannabis experimentation at Year 3 had N = 65 (Discussion p. 5).

primary_models.equation: logit(P(SubstanceExp_Y3[i] = 1)) = b0 + b1*Modality_hours_Y2[i] + b2*SubstanceExp_Y2[i] + b3*age + b4*sex + b5..b9*race_ethnicity + b10..b14*household_income + b15*parent_education + b16*family_conflict + b17*COI_z + site terms; OR = exp(b1) per additional hour/day of the modality. Fitted separately for each outcome (alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, any) and, as presented, for each modality.
primary_models.estimation: Stata 18 (StataCorp). Multiple logistic regression with ABCD sampling weights based on the American Community Survey. Adjusted odds ratios with 95% CIs. Benjamini-Hochberg false discovery rate correction across tests; asterisks in Fig. 1 mark significance after correction. No p-values printed. Effect modification by sex and by race and ethnicity was tested; the Results state there was no evidence of effect modification, and no stratified estimates are reported. No sensitivity analyses reported.

d_transformation.conversion_formula: d = ln(OR) * sqrt(3) / pi (Chinn 2000), applied to the OR and to each CI bound.
d_transformation.contrast_type: per 1 additional hour/day of the Year 2 modality (texting, social media, or video chat)
d_transformation.notes: The ORs are per hour/day, so the Chinn d is a per-1-hour contrast, not a per-SD contrast. Year 2 SD_IV values come from Table 1 (p. 3): texting 1.5, social media 1.6, video chat 1.3 hours/day; these can be used to rescale ln(OR) to a per-SD contrast if needed (ln(OR) x SD_IV). p0 values are the weighted marginal Year 3 prevalences from Table 2 (p. 3), not unexposed-group rates; they are not needed for the OR -> d conversion. Outcomes are rare (nicotine 2.5%, cannabis 1.0% at Year 3; cannabis N = 65), so ORs approximate risk ratios. All values were read from the printed labels on the Fig. 1 forest plot, and 11 of the 12 also appear verbatim in the Results text (video chat -> alcohol appears only in the figure). No p-values are reported. Completion pass (2026-10-01): re-read all 7 PDF pages; all 12 ORs and CIs confirmed against Fig. 1; no SEs or exact p-values exist in the paper; no supplement file bundled. iv_type set to continuous.

extraction_flags:
It holds one model (M1) with 12 estimates: 3 IVs (texting, social media, video chat) by 4 outcomes (alcohol, nicotine, cannabis, any substance). All 12 ORs and CIs were checked against a zoomed render of Fig. 1, and they match.

What a human should verify:
(1) Every estimate comes from the printed labels on the Fig. 1 forest plot. The paper has no results table. 11 of the 12 also appear in the Results text, but video chat -> alcohol (OR 1.04, CI 0.98-1.11, not significant) appears only in the figure. The figure label for texting -> alcohol is missing its opening parenthesis.
(2) The paper prints no p-values. "sig" comes from the Fig. 1 asterisk, which marks significance after Benjamini-Hochberg correction. p is null and p_label is "*" when significant.
(3) The paper never says whether each modality was fitted in its own model or all modalities were entered together. I assumed one modality per model.
(4) Study site is listed as a covariate, but the paper doesn't say whether it is a fixed or random effect.
(5) The ABCD release version is not stated in the PDF. Appendix A, which compares included and excluded participants, is an online supplement and was not in the PDF.
(6) The p0 values are weighted marginal Year 3 prevalences from Table 2. They are not unexposed-group rates, and the OR conversion doesn't need them.
(7) The derived d is per 1 hour/day, not per SD. Year 2 SD_IV values from Table 1 (texting 1.5, social media 1.6, video chat 1.3) are recorded in case they are needed.
(8) Cannabis at Year 3 is rare (N=65, 1.0%).
